questions.stem: A 71-year-old client with type 2 diabetes, heart failure and a baseline creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL had a CT scan of the abdomen with IV contrast 48 hours ago. The client's metformin was continued. Today the creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL, urine output has been 15 to 20 mL/hr for 6 hours, and the client is nauseated and short of breath with a respiratory rate of 26/min. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.24 and lactate 5.8 mmol/L. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

condition.text: Contrast-associated acute kidney injury with metformin-associated lactic acidosis
Delayed allergic reaction to the contrast dye
Acute exacerbation of heart failure alone

actions.text: Hold the metformin and notify the provider of the results
Prepare for treatment of the acidosis, which may include dialysis
Give a large IV fluid bolus quickly to flush the kidneys
Give a dose of oral ibuprofen for the client's discomfort
Schedule a repeat CT with contrast to look for the cause

rationale.correct: Contrast can injure the kidneys within 48 to 72 hours, especially with diabetes, CKD and heart failure. Metformin is held around contrast in at-risk clients because kidney failure can cause lactic acidosis.

perOption.c1: A rise in creatinine within 48 hours of contrast, low urine output and lactic acidosis in a client still taking metformin fit this picture.
perOption.c2: DKA causes marked hyperglycemia and ketones; the high lactate and timing after contrast point elsewhere.
perOption.c3: Allergic reactions cause hives, itching or wheezing, not a rising creatinine and lactic acidosis.
perOption.c4: Shortness of breath may be fluid, but heart failure alone does not explain the acidosis and timing.
perOption.a1: Metformin builds up when the kidneys fail and worsens lactic acidosis.
perOption.a2: Severe metformin-associated lactic acidosis can need dialysis to remove the drug and correct the acidosis.
perOption.a3: The client has heart failure and is short of breath; fluids must be given with care as prescribed.
perOption.a4: NSAIDs further reduce kidney blood flow.
perOption.a5: More contrast would worsen the kidney injury.
perOption.p1: Show whether kidney function is recovering or worsening.
perOption.p2: Show whether the acidosis is responding to treatment.
perOption.p3: Not a key guide to this condition.
perOption.p4: Not related to kidney injury or acidosis.
perOption.p5: Skin turgor is unreliable in older adults and does not guide this treatment.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes who received insulin glargine last night has been NPO since midnight for surgery that has been delayed until afternoon. At 1100 the client is sweaty, shaky and says, "I feel strange and can't think straight." What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Check the client's fingerstick blood glucose right away
Give the client a cup of orange juice, since the surgery is delayed anyway
Tell the client the feelings are probably anxiety about the delayed surgery
Notify the surgeon that the client is too unwell to have surgery today

rationale.correct: Sweating, tremor, confusion and hunger in a client on insulin who is fasting suggest hypoglycemia; check glucose and treat by the protocol for NPO clients.

perOption.a: Sweating, shakiness and confusion in a fasting client on insulin suggest hypoglycemia; confirming it guides treatment.
perOption.b: Oral intake may be needed, but the client is NPO for surgery and the glucose should be checked first.
perOption.c: Assuming anxiety can miss dangerous hypoglycemia.
perOption.d: The client needs assessment and possible treatment before decisions about surgery.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
American Diabetes Association Standards of Care

questions.stem: A client with alcohol use disorder is on telemetry. Morning labs show magnesium 1.1 mg/dL and potassium 3.2 mEq/L. The telemetry strip shows a prolonged QT interval of 0.52 seconds. Which complication is the client at greatest risk for?

options.text: Third-degree heart block with a slow junctional escape rhythm
Torsades de pointes, a form of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia
Atrial flutter with a regular rate of about 150 beats per minute
Sinus bradycardia caused by increased vagal tone while the client is asleep at night

rationale.correct: Hypomagnesemia and hypokalemia prolong the QT interval and can cause torsades de pointes, which is treated with IV magnesium.

perOption.a: Low magnesium and potassium do not typically cause complete heart block.
perOption.b: Low magnesium and potassium with a long QT interval greatly raise the risk of torsades de pointes.
perOption.c: Electrolyte problems can cause atrial dysrhythmias, but a long QT points to torsades.
perOption.d: Bradycardia is not the main risk of these findings.

questions.stem: A client in active labor at 6 cm has a fetal heart rate baseline of 140/min with moderate variability. The nurse sees abrupt, V-shaped drops in the fetal heart rate to 90/min that vary in timing with contractions and return quickly to baseline. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Increase the oxytocin infusion to speed the labor along
Change the client's position, such as to the side or hands and knees
Prepare the client for an emergency cesarean birth right away
Document the pattern as expected for active labor and keep monitoring

rationale.correct: Variable decelerations come from cord compression; reposition the client, stop oxytocin if it is running and decelerations persist, and notify the provider.

perOption.a: Oxytocin increases contraction strength and can worsen cord compression.
perOption.b: These are variable decelerations from cord compression; changing position often relieves the pressure on the cord.
perOption.c: Variable decelerations with moderate variability are first managed with position changes.
perOption.d: Variable decelerations need intervention, even if the variability is reassuring.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client at 36 weeks with gestational hypertension has a nonstress test. Over 20 minutes, the fetal heart rate rises at least 15 beats/min above the baseline for at least 15 seconds three times, each with fetal movement. How should the nurse interpret this result?

options.text: Nonreactive; the fetus may be compromised and needs a biophysical profile
Reactive; the fetus is likely well oxygenated at this time
Positive; contractions are causing late decelerations in the fetal heart rate
Inconclusive; the test needs to be repeated after the client eats a meal

rationale.correct: A reactive nonstress test (accelerations of at least 15 beats/min for 15 seconds, twice in 20 minutes after 32 weeks) is reassuring.

perOption.a: These accelerations meet the criteria for a reactive test.
perOption.b: Two or more accelerations of at least 15 beats/min for 15 seconds in 20 minutes after 32 weeks is a reactive, reassuring result.
perOption.c: A positive result describes a contraction stress test with late decelerations.
perOption.d: The test met its criteria and is not inconclusive.

questions.stem: A client had a total knee replacement yesterday. The client's pain is 8 of 10, and the client asks to skip physical therapy today. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Agree that the client can skip therapy until the pain is below 3 of 10
Give the prescribed analgesic about 30 minutes before therapy and encourage the session
Tell the client that pain after knee surgery is normal and therapy cannot be skipped
Keep the knee resting on a pillow so that it stays bent and comfortable for the whole day

rationale.correct: After joint replacement, time analgesia before therapy and promote early mobility; avoid pillows under the knee.

perOption.a: Delaying mobility increases stiffness, clots and complications.
perOption.b: Pain control before therapy makes exercise possible; early motion is vital to recovery after knee replacement.
perOption.c: This dismisses the client's pain without treating it.
perOption.d: A pillow under the knee promotes a flexion contracture.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: A 22-year-old client with a closed femur fracture from a motorcycle crash is in skeletal traction. Thirty-six hours after the injury, the client becomes restless and confused, the respiratory rate is 32/min, SpO2 is 86% and the nurse sees tiny red-purple spots across the chest and in the armpits. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Alcohol withdrawal starting 36 hours after the client's last drink
Fat embolism syndrome
A reaction to the opioid that is being given for pain
Compartment syndrome of the injured thigh

rationale.correct: Fat embolism syndrome follows long-bone fractures within 24 to 72 hours: hypoxemia, confusion and petechiae. Give oxygen, support breathing and notify the provider.

perOption.a: Withdrawal can cause confusion and restlessness, but not hypoxemia with a petechial rash.
perOption.b: Respiratory distress, confusion and petechiae on the chest and axillae 24 to 72 hours after a long-bone fracture are classic fat embolism.
perOption.c: Opioid effects slow breathing and do not cause petechiae.
perOption.d: Compartment syndrome causes limb pain and changes, not breathing problems and a rash on the chest.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is starting a 24-hour urine collection for creatinine clearance at 0800. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Have the client void at 0800, discard that urine and record the start time
Keep the collection container on ice or refrigerated as the lab directs
Save the first void at 0800 to start the collection
Ask the client to void at 0800 the next day and add that urine to the container
Restart the collection if one void is thrown away by mistake
Collect only the urine passed during the day while the client is awake

rationale.correct: 24-hour urine: discard the first void, collect all urine for 24 hours, keep it cold, include the final void and restart if any is lost.

perOption.a: The test starts with an empty bladder, so the first void is discarded.
perOption.b: Cold storage prevents breakdown of substances in the urine.
perOption.c: Urine made before the start time would add to the total and give a wrong result.
perOption.d: The final void completes the 24 hours.
perOption.e: A missed sample makes the test inaccurate.
perOption.f: The test needs all urine over 24 hours.

questions.stem: During a preoperative interview for an elective hip replacement in 1 week, a client says they take ginkgo biloba, garlic capsules and fish oil every day. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the client that natural supplements are safe and can be continued
Report the supplements to the surgeon, since they can increase bleeding risk
Tell the client to double the fish oil before surgery to protect the heart
Write the supplements down but leave them out of the client's medication list

rationale.correct: Ask about herbal supplements before surgery; ginkgo, garlic, ginseng, fish oil and vitamin E can increase bleeding and are reported to the surgeon.

perOption.a: Several supplements affect bleeding and anesthesia.
perOption.b: Ginkgo, garlic and fish oil can increase bleeding; they are often stopped before surgery as directed.
perOption.c: Extra fish oil would increase bleeding risk.
perOption.d: Supplements belong on the medication list because they interact with drugs and surgery.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old client who ran out of clonidine 3 days ago comes to the emergency department with a severe headache, blurred vision and confusion. Blood pressure is 232/134 mm Hg in both arms, and the client vomited twice. There is no weakness or facial droop, and a CT of the head shows no bleeding. Urine shows protein and blood. Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Start a titrated IV antihypertensive such as nicardipine as prescribed
Lower the mean arterial pressure by no more than about 25% in the first hour
Give sublingual nifedipine to bring the pressure down to normal quickly
Wait for the blood pressure to settle on its own after the client rests
Give the missed clonidine doses all at once to catch up

parameters.text: Blood pressure every 5 to 15 minutes, by arterial line if available
Neurological status, including level of consciousness and vision
Oral temperature checked every 4 hours with the routine vital signs
Bowel sounds listened for in each of the four abdominal quadrants
Body weight measured on the same scale each morning before breakfast

rationale.correct: Hypertensive emergency means severe hypertension with organ damage. Lower the pressure in a controlled way with titrated IV drugs (about 25% in the first hour) and monitor blood pressure and neurological status.

perOption.c1: Severe hypertension with headache, confusion, vision changes and signs of kidney injury is a hypertensive emergency; stopping clonidine causes rebound hypertension.
perOption.c2: Confusion, vision changes and protein in the urine show organ damage, which makes this an emergency.
perOption.c3: There are no focal deficits, and the CT is clear; the confusion is from hypertensive encephalopathy.
perOption.c4: Migraine does not cause a blood pressure of 232/134 with kidney changes.
perOption.a1: IV drugs allow controlled, steady lowering of blood pressure.
perOption.a2: Lowering pressure too fast can cause stroke or kidney and heart ischemia.
perOption.a3: Rapid, unpredictable drops can cause stroke and are avoided.
perOption.a4: Organ damage is happening now; treatment must start at once.
perOption.a5: Large catch-up doses are unsafe and do not provide controlled lowering.
perOption.p1: Close monitoring prevents both overshoot and undertreatment.
perOption.p2: Shows whether the encephalopathy is improving or a stroke is developing.
perOption.p3: Not a key parameter for hypertensive emergency.
perOption.p5: Daily weight does not guide acute blood pressure treatment.

Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student is admitted with fever, severe headache, a stiff neck and a purple rash on the legs that does not blanch. Bacterial meningitis is suspected. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Wait to start antibiotics until the lumbar puncture results confirm the organism
Place the client on droplet precautions and prepare to give IV antibiotics right away
Put the client in a brightly lit room so the nurse can watch the rash closely
Ask the client's roommates to visit so they can help keep the client calm and oriented

rationale.correct: Suspected bacterial meningitis with a petechial rash: droplet precautions, immediate IV antibiotics, seizure precautions and prophylaxis for close contacts.

perOption.a: Delaying antibiotics in suspected bacterial meningitis increases death and disability.
perOption.b: A petechial rash suggests meningococcal disease; droplet precautions protect others and antibiotics are given without delay.
perOption.c: Clients with meningitis are often light-sensitive; a dim, quiet room is better.
perOption.d: Close contacts need assessment for prophylaxis, not visits during the infectious period.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
CDC infection control and isolation precautions guidance

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing clients with heart failure. For each finding, indicate whether it is more typical of left-sided or right-sided heart failure.

rows.text: Swelling of the ankles and legs
Needing three pillows to breathe at night
Distended neck veins with the head raised 45 degrees
Enlarged, tender liver and loss of appetite

rationale.correct: Left-sided failure affects the lungs (crackles, dyspnea, orthopnea); right-sided failure affects the body (edema, distended neck veins, hepatomegaly).

perOption.r1:c1: Fluid backs up into the lungs when the left ventricle fails.
perOption.r1:c2: Right-sided failure causes systemic, not lung, congestion.
perOption.r2:c1: Leg swelling is mainly from systemic venous congestion.
perOption.r2:c2: Right-sided failure backs blood up into the body's veins.
perOption.r3:c1: Orthopnea comes from fluid in the lungs.
perOption.r3:c2: Orthopnea is a sign of pulmonary congestion.
perOption.r4:c1: Jugular distention reflects high right-sided pressure.
perOption.r5:c1: These come from venous congestion of the liver and gut.
perOption.r5:c2: Right-sided failure congests the abdominal organs.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with acute pulmonary edema has a prescription for furosemide 80 mg IV. Which action is most important when the nurse gives this dose?

options.text: Push the full dose rapidly over 10 seconds so it works faster
Give it slowly, about 20 mg per minute or less, and check the potassium
Mix the dose into a liter of IV fluid and run it over 8 hours
Hold the dose if the client's blood pressure is above 140/90 mm Hg on the next check

rationale.correct: IV furosemide: give slowly to prevent ototoxicity, monitor potassium, blood pressure, urine output and weight.

perOption.a: Rapid IV furosemide can cause hearing loss; it is given slowly, about 20 mg/min or less.
perOption.b: A slow rate protects hearing, and furosemide causes potassium loss that must be monitored.
perOption.c: This would deliver extra fluid and delay the diuretic effect the client needs now.
perOption.d: High blood pressure is not a reason to hold furosemide in pulmonary edema.

questions.stem: Review the 0700 findings. Highlight the findings that require immediate follow-up.

rationale.correct: Hypotension, tachycardia, low urine output and Cullen's sign point to severe pancreatitis with fluid shifts and bleeding.

perOption.s2: Cullen's sign suggests bleeding into the abdomen in severe pancreatitis.
perOption.s4: A position of comfort that is common in pancreatitis.
perOption.s6: Falling blood pressure suggests fluid loss into the abdomen.
perOption.s8: Rising heart rate is compensation for hypovolemia.
perOption.s10: Low urine output shows poor kidney perfusion.
perOption.s12: Confirms the diagnosis but does not itself need a new action.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize cues of severe acute pancreatitis.

questions.stem: Complete the sentence based on the client's data.

content.template: The client's falling blood pressure and rising hematocrit are most likely caused by {{b1}}, and the low calcium is a sign of {{b2}}.

options.text: fluid shifting out of the blood vessels into the abdomen
a reaction to the pain medication
an acute myocardial infarction
severe pancreatitis, as fat breakdown binds calcium
a dietary calcium deficiency
parathyroid gland overactivity

rationale.correct: Severe pancreatitis causes third-spacing of fluid (hypovolemia, rising hematocrit) and hypocalcemia from fat necrosis.

perOption.b1:a: Inflammation makes vessels leaky; fluid loss concentrates the blood and lowers blood pressure.
perOption.b1:b: Pain medication does not raise the hematocrit.
perOption.b1:c: The picture fits fluid loss from pancreatitis.
perOption.b2:a: Fatty acids released in pancreatitis bind calcium, and low calcium predicts more severe disease.
perOption.b2:b: Acute hypocalcemia here is from the disease process, not diet.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: For each potential complication, indicate whether the client is at high or low immediate risk based on the current data.

rows.text: Tetany or seizures from low calcium

rationale.correct: Severe pancreatitis threatens circulation, breathing and electrolyte balance; glucose is usually high, not low.

perOption.r1:c1: Falling blood pressure, tachycardia and low urine output show shock is developing.
perOption.r1:c2: The data show a high risk.
perOption.r2:c1: Calcium of 7.4 mg/dL can cause tetany and dysrhythmias.
perOption.r2:c2: The low calcium makes this risk high.
perOption.r3:c1: Rising respiratory rate in severe pancreatitis can signal ARDS.
perOption.r3:c2: The tachypnea makes this risk high.
perOption.r4:c1: The glucose is high, not low.
perOption.r4:c2: Glucose is 228 mg/dL, so the immediate risk is low.

questions.stem: Which interventions should the nurse anticipate for this client? Select all that apply.

options.text: Aggressive IV fluid replacement with isotonic crystalloid as prescribed
Keep the client NPO and give IV opioids for pain as prescribed
Check for Chvostek's and Trousseau's signs and have IV calcium available
Start a high-fat oral diet to restore calories quickly
Monitor oxygen saturation and breathing closely
Give a dose of the prescribed alcohol-containing cough syrup at bedtime

rationale.correct: Pancreatitis care: fluids, NPO with early enteral feeding as tolerated, pain control, monitoring calcium, glucose and breathing, and no alcohol.

perOption.a: Fluid restores volume lost to third-spacing and protects the kidneys.
perOption.b: Resting the gut and treating severe pain are core treatments.
perOption.c: These signs detect hypocalcemia that may need replacement.
perOption.d: Fat stimulates the pancreas and worsens pain.
perOption.e: ARDS and pleural effusions are complications.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.stem: The client rates pain 9 of 10 and has a prescription for hydromorphone 1 mg IV every 2 hours as needed. The last dose was 2 hours ago. The respiratory rate is 28/min, and the client is alert. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Hold the dose because opioids will worsen the client's pancreatitis
Give the hydromorphone and reassess pain and sedation within 15 to 30 minutes
Offer acetaminophen instead, since the pain is not yet severe enough for an opioid
Wait until the pain reaches 10 of 10 before giving the next dose of IV hydromorphone to the client

rationale.correct: Severe pancreatitis pain is treated with IV opioids; reassess pain, sedation and breathing after each dose.

perOption.a: Opioids are appropriate for pancreatitis pain; uncontrolled pain increases stress and oxygen demand.
perOption.b: The client is alert with a fast respiratory rate; treating severe pain and reassessing is appropriate.
perOption.c: Pain of 9 of 10 is severe and needs stronger analgesia.
perOption.d: Waiting allows pain to escalate and is harder to control.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

content.template: The client's findings are most consistent with {{b1}}, and the client's risk factors include {{b2}}.

options.text: pulmonary embolism
postoperative pneumonia
an anxiety attack
cancer, recent pelvic surgery, immobility and missed enoxaparin

rationale.correct: Cancer, pelvic surgery, immobility and missed prophylaxis are major risk factors for PE.

perOption.b1:a: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic pain, hypoxemia and tachycardia with a DVT fit PE.
perOption.b1:b: Pneumonia develops more gradually with fever and productive cough.
perOption.b1:c: Anxiety does not cause an SpO2 of 86% or calf swelling.

questions.educationalObjective: Analyze cues and risk factors for pulmonary embolism.

questions.stem: Complete the diagram by placing the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.

actions.text: Give oxygen and raise the head of the bed
Notify the provider or rapid response team at once
Massage the left calf to relieve the tenderness
Help the client walk in the hall to improve breathing
Give the prescribed oral pain medicine and reassess in an hour

parameters.text: Bowel sounds in each of the four abdominal quadrants
Amount and color of drainage on the abdominal incision dressing
Color and clarity of the urine in the collection bag

rationale.correct: Suspected PE: oxygen, head of bed up, rapid response, anticoagulation as prescribed, and close monitoring of oxygenation and blood pressure.

perOption.c1: Sudden pleuritic pain, hypoxemia, tachycardia and a DVT after surgery indicate PE.
perOption.c2: Chest pain is present, but pleuritic pain with a DVT and hypoxemia points to PE.
perOption.c3: Nothing suggests a punctured lung, and the calf findings point to a clot.
perOption.c4: Atelectasis does not cause sudden severe hypoxemia with pleuritic pain on day 4.
perOption.a1: Oxygen corrects hypoxemia and sitting up eases breathing.
perOption.a2: PE is an emergency that needs imaging and anticoagulation.
perOption.a4: Walking with an acute PE and hypoxemia is unsafe.
perOption.p1: Show whether oxygenation is improving or worsening.
perOption.p2: Falling blood pressure can signal a massive PE.

questions.stem: Which interventions should the nurse anticipate after the provider evaluates the client? Select all that apply.

options.text: A CT pulmonary angiogram to confirm the diagnosis
Starting an anticoagulant such as a heparin infusion as prescribed
Continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring
Applying a sequential compression device to the left leg
Keeping the client on bed rest with the legs raised high on pillows

rationale.correct: PE workup and treatment: CT angiography, anticoagulation and monitoring; avoid compression devices on a leg with acute DVT.

perOption.a: CT angiography is the main test for PE.
perOption.b: Anticoagulation stops the clot from growing.
perOption.c: Monitoring detects worsening oxygenation and rhythm changes.
perOption.d: Compression on a leg with an acute DVT may dislodge clot.
perOption.e: Strict bed rest with raised legs is not standard; activity is guided by the provider once anticoagulated.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

questions.educationalObjective: Plan care after pulmonary embolism is suspected.

questions.stem: The client is started on a weight-based heparin infusion. Six hours later, the aPTT is 118 seconds; the protocol target is 60 to 90 seconds. There is no bleeding. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue the infusion at the same rate and recheck the aPTT in the morning
Follow the protocol, which may mean pausing the infusion and lowering the rate
Give protamine sulfate right away to reverse the heparin completely
Increase the rate, since a higher aPTT means the clot is dissolving faster

rationale.correct: Adjust heparin infusions by the aPTT or anti-Xa protocol; above-range results usually mean a brief hold and a lower rate, with a recheck.

perOption.a: An aPTT above the target increases bleeding risk and needs adjustment now.
perOption.b: Heparin protocols direct the nurse to hold briefly and reduce the rate when the aPTT is above range.
perOption.c: Protamine is for serious bleeding or overdose, not a high aPTT without bleeding.
perOption.d: Heparin does not dissolve clots; a high aPTT means too much anticoagulation.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.educationalObjective: Adjust a heparin infusion by protocol.

questions.stem: Two days later, the nurse reassesses the client. For each finding, indicate whether it shows improvement or needs follow-up.

rows.text: Chest pain 2 of 10 with deep breathing

rationale.correct: Better oxygenation, heart rate and pain show recovery; signs of bleeding on anticoagulation need prompt reporting.

perOption.r4:c1: Black stools suggest GI bleeding from anticoagulation.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)

exhibits.title: Medical unit, 0700
exhibits.body: A 47-year-old client was admitted last night with severe epigastric pain that goes through to the back, after a weekend of heavy drinking. The client is lying curled on the side and has vomited three times. The abdomen is tender with guarding and decreased bowel sounds. The nurse notes a bluish discoloration around the umbilicus.

exhibits.title: Surgical unit, day 4 after surgery, 1400
exhibits.body: A 63-year-old client is 4 days after a total abdominal hysterectomy for cancer. The client has walked little because of pain and refused enoxaparin injections twice. The client suddenly reports sharp chest pain that is worse with breathing in and feels anxious, saying "something is wrong." The left calf is swollen and tender.

testSets.title: NCLEX-RN adaptive exam
testSets.description: Works like the real NCLEX-RN: each question depends on your answers so far, and the exam stops once your result is clear, after 85 to 150 questions. Choose timed (5 hours) or untimed. No going back; answers and rationales at the end. The questions are being rewritten to real NCLEX difficulty and recalibrated, so treat your result as a practice estimate.
